account.name: Brightwave Logistics
account.industry: transportation, logistics, supply chain and storage

dossier.summary: Brightwave Logistics is a freight and logistics company with about 420 people and a regional cross-dock network.
dossier.why_now: Opened two cross-dock sites this year.

data.speakers: Priya Natarajan, Daniel Okafor and Maya Chen.

chapters.title: Who was on the call
chapters.summary: Introductions and what the session covers.

chapters.title: Where the hours go: the time audit of 40 teams
chapters.summary: A time audit of 40 operations teams. The median was 31 hours per 100 loads across four areas. Teams that had added sites sat at 36 to 40.

chapters.title: The three handoffs that cost the most hours
chapters.summary: Dispatch to billing, exceptions and customer updates were the three handoffs that cost the most hours.

chapters.title: Kestrel's year: 28% more loads, the same 60 people
chapters.summary: Kestrel's loads grew 28 percent year on year while its operations team went from 61 people to 60.

chapters.title: What Kestrel changed first: one desk for exceptions
chapters.summary: Kestrel moved exception handling to one desk before touching dispatch. It gave back the most hours per month of any change.

chapters.title: Questions: exceptions, customer updates, planner roles
chapters.summary: Asked about a new cross-dock, Priya said to run it from the central desk for a quarter before hiring a planner.

chapters.title: Close and the audit template
chapters.summary: Wrap up and where to get the audit template.

slide_pages.caption: The audit sheet, hours per 100 loads

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: So the number everyone asks about is the 28 percent. Loads were up 28 percent year on year, and the operations team was 61 people in January and 60 in December. One person left and we did not backfill. That was not a plan, it just happened, and then we noticed nothing broke.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: What made it possible was not one thing. It was three handoffs, in order. Dispatch to billing first, because that is where the hours were and the fix was boring. Exceptions second. Customer updates last, and that one we got wrong the first time.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: What went wrong the first time?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: We automated the update before we agreed what an update was. Every terminal had its own idea. So customers got three messages for one late truck. We pulled it after two weeks, wrote the definition down, and the second version stuck.

data.book_title: Want the audit run on your numbers?
data.book_text: Maya can walk your dispatch and billing leads through the sheet in 20 minutes. You keep the sheet either way.

takeaways.title: Run the audit on dispatch and billing first
takeaways.body: The median across 40 teams was 31 hours per 100 loads. Teams that had added sites sat at 36 to 40, and Brightwave opened two cross-dock sites this year.

takeaways.title: Centralize exceptions before anything else
takeaways.body: Kestrel moved exception handling to one desk before touching dispatch. It gave back the most hours per month of any change, which matters most when volume is growing.

takeaways.title: A new site does not need a planner on day one
takeaways.body: Priya's answer on new cross-docks was to run the site from the central desk for a quarter, then decide. With two sites opened this year, that is a live question for operations.
